advances: The parity midpoint channel gives an exact entropy-energy-relative-entropy identity and proves the unrestricted scalar entropy-energy inequality with least strictly positive universal coefficient one. A rational planar convex-body family proves sharpness against every feasible array. The same channel gives simultaneous full original-incidence capacities and an exact total logarithmic cost for all its pair and singleton components. Its complete target support and an explicit failure of row log-concavity identify limits of this construction; the all-target mass calculation does not supply a single-target hitting or depth bound for the locked problem.

proof:
Accepted fact `488f0a583886b5fc` supplies completeness of \(D\), convex-admissibility of the original potential \(\phi\), and the full-incidence component convention and original logarithmic costs used above. Convex-admissibility applied to each positive row of any \(r\in\mathcal F(p)\) gives \(q_{\mathbf J}\phi_{\mathbf J}\le\sum_{\mathbf I}r_{\mathbf J,\mathbf I}\phi_{\mathbf I}\); summing proves \(G(r)\ge0\) for globally extendable tables. Zero rows contribute zero. The diagonal array proves that the feasible set is nonempty, including a one-point support.

For the explicit construction, sample a parity class \(\mathbf B\) with law \(\pi\), omitting its zero-mass classes. Conditional on \(\mathbf B=\mathbf b\), sample \(\mathbf X,\mathbf Y\) independently with probabilities \(p_{\mathbf I}/\pi_{\mathbf b}\) on that class. Both unconditional source marginals equal \(p\). Their midpoint \(\mathbf J=(\mathbf X+\mathbf Y)/2\) is integral, and midpoint positivity places it in \(D\). The joint law of \((\mathbf J,\mathbf X)\) is exactly the displayed array, with zero contribution from a reflected endpoint outside \(D\).

For fixed \(\mathbf I\), the reflected endpoint \(\mathbf K=2\mathbf J-\mathbf I\) runs bijectively over its entire same-parity positive support as the nonzero terms in that column are summed. Thus the column sum is \(p_{\mathbf I}\). Exchangeability of \((\mathbf X,\mathbf Y)\), preserved upon conditioning on their midpoint, gives \(\mathbb E[\mathbf X\mid\mathbf J]=\mathbf J\), so the row identities hold. Also \(r_{\mathbf J,\mathbf J}=p_{\mathbf J}^2/\pi_{\mathbf J\bmod2}>0\) for every \(\mathbf J\in D\), proving exact full target support.

Write conditional Shannon entropies of random variables as \(\operatorname{Ent}(\cdot\mid\cdot)\). For fixed \(\mathbf X\), the map \(\mathbf Y\mapsto\mathbf J\) is injective, and the conditional law of \(\mathbf Y\) depends on \(\mathbf X\) only through its parity. Consequently,

\[
\begin{aligned}
H(r)&=\operatorname{Ent}(\mathbf J\mid\mathbf X)
=\operatorname{Ent}(\mathbf Y\mid\mathbf B)\\
&=-\sum_{\mathbf b:\pi_{\mathbf b}>0}\sum_{\mathbf I\equiv\mathbf b\pmod2}
p_{\mathbf I}\log\frac{p_{\mathbf I}}{\pi_{\mathbf b}}
=S(p)-S(\pi),\\
I(r)&=S(q)-S(p)+S(\pi).
\end{aligned}
\]

Using the original column sums and cancellation of the constant \(\log p_{\max}\), direct expansion gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
G(r)&=S(p)+\sum_{\mathbf J}q_{\mathbf J}\log p_{\mathbf J},\\
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p)&=-S(q)-\sum_{\mathbf J}q_{\mathbf J}\log p_{\mathbf J}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Adding the three formulas proves the exact identity. The same expansion also verifies the stated mutual-information formula for every feasible array. Relative entropy is nonnegative: for probability laws \(u,v\) with \(v>0\) wherever \(u>0\), the inequality \(\log t\le t-1\) gives
\(\sum_{u_x>0}u_x\log(u_x/v_x)\ge1-\sum_{u_x>0}v_x\ge0\).
Apply this to \(q,p\) and to the joint law \(r\) versus the product law \(q\otimes p\). Applying it to \(\pi\) versus the uniform law on \(2^n\) classes gives \(S(\pi)\le n\log2\). Thus dropping the relative-entropy term proves the required scalar bound. For the weaker midpoint hypotheses, nonnegativity of the explicit array's energy follows directly from
\(G(r)=\mathbb E[(\phi_{\mathbf X}+\phi_{\mathbf Y})/2-\phi_{(\mathbf X+\mathbf Y)/2}]\ge0\).
Every other construction step used only midpoint closure, finite probability identities, or this midpoint inequality. This proves the asserted weakening without requiring convex-admissibility for arbitrary rows under that weakening.

Each distinct pair is an affinely independent barycentric component at its midpoint, and each singleton is the central component at its own target. For a fixed source \(\mathbf I\) in parity class \(\mathbf b\), its full usage across all components is

\[
\frac{w_{\mathbf I}^2}{W_{\mathbf b}}
+\sum_{\substack{\mathbf K\ne\mathbf I\\\mathbf K\equiv\mathbf b\pmod2}}
\frac{w_{\mathbf I}w_{\mathbf K}}{W_{\mathbf b}}
=\frac{w_{\mathbf I}}{W_{\mathbf b}}
\sum_{\mathbf K\equiv\mathbf b\pmod2}w_{\mathbf K}
=w_{\mathbf I}.
\]

No barycentric coefficient discounts this charge. The ordered sum of \(w_{\mathbf I}w_{\mathbf K}/W_{\mathbf b}\) over each nonempty class is \(W_{\mathbf b}\). Passing to unordered pairs and retaining each diagonal once gives the formula for \(M_{\mathrm{all}}\). In each class, \(\sum_{\mathbf I\equiv\mathbf b}w_{\mathbf I}^2\le W_{\mathbf b}^2\), so the diagonal sum lies between zero and \(W\), giving the stated mass bounds.

For a distinct pair at \(\mathbf J\), its two array entries are both \(x_E/W\). Their combined contribution to \(G(r)\) is
\((x_E/W)(\phi_{\mathbf I}+\phi_{\mathbf K}-2\phi_{\mathbf J})=(2x_E/W)G_E\).
Singleton entries contribute zero. Summation proves the cost equality and hence its information-theoretic expression and upper bound.

For actual positive-volume fibers, let \(\nu_{\mathbf I}=\mathcal L^d|_{C_{\mathbf I}}/w_{\mathbf I}\). A pair component can be the measure \(x_E(\nu_{\mathbf I}\otimes\nu_{\mathbf K})\), and a singleton can be \(x_E\nu_{\mathbf I}\). Both pair source marginals have the full mass \(x_E\), and convexity places their geometric midpoints in the fiber at \((\mathbf I+\mathbf K)/2\). At every source, the sum of its incident marginals is \((\sum_{E:\mathbf I\in E}x_E)\nu_{\mathbf I}=\mathcal L^d|_{C_{\mathbf I}}\), as asserted. These components have different integer targets; none of the equalities makes their total mass a packing at one target.

We next prove all-array sharpness. For the specified dyadic \(\varepsilon\), let \(a_\varepsilon\) be the linear interpolation of the four positive heights \(p_{-1},p_0,p_1,p_2\) on \([-1,2]\). Its successive slopes are \((1-2\varepsilon)/2,0,-(1-2\varepsilon)/2\), which are nonincreasing since \(\varepsilon<1/2\). Therefore
\(C_\varepsilon=\{(t,y):-1\le t\le2,\ 0\le y\le a_\varepsilon(t)\}\)
is a compact convex polygon with nonempty interior and rational vertices. Its only integer fibers occur at \(-1,0,1,2\), with exactly the four specified lengths and total mixed volume one. The interpolation is positive and concave, hence log-concave by the weighted arithmetic-geometric mean inequality; its zero extension outside the interval is globally log-concave. Thus this table meets the complete-table hypotheses exactly.

Now let \((J,X)\) have any feasible joint law \(r\) for this table. Put \(a=\Pr(J\in\{-1,2\})\) and \(\delta=\varepsilon-a\). Since \(X\ge-1\), the row mean equation at \(J=-1\) forces \(X=-1\) throughout that row; likewise \(J=2\) forces \(X=2\). These statements include zero boundary rows. Consequently \(0\le a\le\varepsilon\) and \(0\le\delta\le\varepsilon\); \(\delta\) is precisely the outer-source mass assigned to inner targets. The canonical potential is zero at the inner sites and equals \(B=\log((1-\varepsilon)/\varepsilon)\) at the outer sites. Thus \(G(r)=\delta B\).

Let \(U=\mathbf1_{\{X\ge1\}}\) and \(T=\mathbf1_{\{X\in\{-1,2\}\}}\). The pair \((U,T)\) determines \(X\). Its law makes \(U\) a fair bit independent of the Bernoulli-\(\varepsilon\) bit \(T\), so \(S(p)=\log2+\mathsf h(\varepsilon)\), where \(\mathsf h(u)=-u\log u-(1-u)\log(1-u)\), including its continuous endpoint values.

Predict \(U\) from \(J\) by \(\widehat U=\mathbf1_{\{J\ge1\}}\), and let \(e=\Pr(U\ne\widehat U)\). On row \(J=0\), the mean identity gives \(r_{0,1}+2r_{0,2}=r_{0,-1}\), so its error mass \(r_{0,1}+r_{0,2}\) is at most \(r_{0,-1}\). On row \(J=1\), it gives \(2r_{1,-1}+r_{1,0}=r_{1,2}\), so its error mass \(r_{1,-1}+r_{1,0}\) is at most \(r_{1,2}\). Boundary rows make no error. These two upper bounds together are at most all outer-source mass at inner targets, namely \(\delta\), and hence \(e\le\delta<1/2\).

At a fixed \(J\), the error bit determines \(U\), so concavity of binary entropy gives \(\operatorname{Ent}(U\mid J)\le\mathsf h(e)\le\mathsf h(\delta)\). The second inequality uses monotonicity on \([0,1/2]\). At outer targets \(T=1\) is certain; at inner targets its total mass is \(\delta\) and their total row mass is \(1-a>0\). Concavity therefore gives
\(\operatorname{Ent}(T\mid J)\le(1-a)\mathsf h(\delta/(1-a))\).
The entropy chain rule and conditional subadditivity now yield

\[
\begin{aligned}
I(r)&=S(p)-\operatorname{Ent}(X\mid J)\\
&\ge\log2+\mathsf h(\varepsilon)-\mathsf h(\delta)
-(1-a)\mathsf h\!\left(\frac{\delta}{1-a}\right).
\end{aligned}
\]

Here conditional subadditivity follows by expanding the entropy chain rule and using concavity to see that additional conditioning cannot increase entropy; thus it applies also to deterministic or zero rows.

Put \(\ell=\log(1/\varepsilon)\). The elementary bound \(\mathsf h(u)\le u\log(1/u)+u\) follows from \(-(1-u)\log(1-u)\le u\). If \(\delta=t\varepsilon\) with \(0\le t\le1\), then \(t\log(1/t)\le1\), with the continuous value zero at \(t=0\). Consequently

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathsf h(\varepsilon)&\ge\varepsilon\ell,\\
\mathsf h(\delta)&\le\delta\ell+2\varepsilon,\\
(1-a)\mathsf h\!\left(\frac{\delta}{1-a}\right)
&\le\delta\log\frac{1-a}{\delta}+\delta
\le\delta\ell+2\varepsilon,\\
B&=\ell+\log(1-\varepsilon)\ge\ell-1.
\end{aligned}
\]

The line involving \(\delta\) is interpreted by continuity when \(\delta=0\). The last inequality uses \(\varepsilon<1/2\). Since \(0\le\delta\le\varepsilon\), combining the energy equality and these bounds gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
G(r)+cI(r)-c\log2
&\ge[c\varepsilon+(1-2c)\delta]\ell-(1+4c)\varepsilon\\
&\ge\varepsilon\bigl(\min\{c,1-c\}\ell-(1+4c)\bigr)>0.
\end{aligned}
\]

The final strict inequality is exactly the stipulated choice of \(m\). Rearranging and using \(I(r)=S(q)-H(r)\) proves the claimed strict failure for every feasible array. Since coefficient one always works by the explicit channel and every strictly positive smaller coefficient fails on this rational actual-body family, one is the least strictly positive universal coefficient. At coefficient zero the diagonal array has zero energy, proving the stated exception.

For the five-site example, a globally log-concave extension is the constant \(1/5\) on \([0,4]\) and zero outside; it is also the fiber table of the rectangle \([0,4]\times[0,1/5]\). Its even and odd parity masses are \(3/5\) and \(2/5\). The row at target \(2\) is therefore \((1/15,1/10,1/15,1/10,1/15)\), of mass \(2/5\). Normalizing gives the stated row, which violates midpoint log-concavity at source \(2\), since \((1/6)^2=1/36<1/16=(1/4)^2\). A globally log-concave extension of that normalized row is consequently impossible. All five targets are positive by the diagonal-entry formula, although \(n=1\) and \(2^n=2\). The general full-support conclusion also permits arbitrarily many targets. This completes all asserted construction and sharpness claims.
statement:
Let \(n\ge1\) be an integer, and use the complete-table setting of accepted fact `488f0a583886b5fc`. Thus \(w=(w_{\mathbf I})_{\mathbf I\in\mathbb Z^n}\) is a nonzero, nonnegative, finitely supported table with a finite-valued globally log-concave extension agreeing with every lattice value, including zeros. Write \(D=\{\mathbf I:w_{\mathbf I}>0\}\), \(W=\sum_Dw_{\mathbf I}>0\), \(p_{\mathbf I}=w_{\mathbf I}/W\), and \(p_{\mathbf I}=0\) off \(D\). This is the complete support, with \(D=\operatorname{conv}(D)\cap\mathbb Z^n\); no affine-rank assumption is imposed. Set \(p_{\max}=\max_Dp_{\mathbf I}\) and \(\phi_{\mathbf I}=\log(p_{\max}/p_{\mathbf I})\) on \(D\). All logarithms are natural.

Both indices of an array range over \(D\). Define its feasible set and its row law by

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal F(p)&=\left\{r\ge0:
\sum_{\mathbf J\in D}r_{\mathbf J,\mathbf I}=p_{\mathbf I}\ (\mathbf I\in D),\quad
\sum_{\mathbf I\in D}r_{\mathbf J,\mathbf I}(\mathbf I-\mathbf J)=\mathbf0\ (\mathbf J\in D)\right\},\\
q_{\mathbf J}&=\sum_{\mathbf I\in D}r_{\mathbf J,\mathbf I}.
\end{aligned}
\]

For any finite probability law \(v\), write \(S(v)=-\sum_xv_x\log v_x\), with zero summands interpreted by continuity. For \(r\in\mathcal F(p)\), use the original potential and the following canonical quantities:

\[
\begin{aligned}
H(r)&=-\sum_{\mathbf J,\mathbf I}r_{\mathbf J,\mathbf I}
\log\frac{r_{\mathbf J,\mathbf I}}{p_{\mathbf I}},\\
I(r)&=S(q)-H(r)
=\sum_{\substack{\mathbf J,\mathbf I\\r_{\mathbf J,\mathbf I}>0}}
r_{\mathbf J,\mathbf I}\log\frac{r_{\mathbf J,\mathbf I}}{q_{\mathbf J}p_{\mathbf I}},\\
G(r)&=\sum_{\mathbf J,\mathbf I}r_{\mathbf J,\mathbf I}(\phi_{\mathbf I}-\phi_{\mathbf J}),\\
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p)&=\sum_{\mathbf J:q_{\mathbf J}>0}q_{\mathbf J}\log\frac{q_{\mathbf J}}{p_{\mathbf J}}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus \(H(r)\) is conditional assignment entropy, not the Shannon entropy \(S(q)\). In the archived first response of `advance-oertel.txt`, \(\mathcal A,\mathcal I,\mathcal G,\mathsf H\) are respectively \(H,I,G,S\) here, and its potential \(-\log p_{\mathbf I}\) equals \(\phi_{\mathbf I}-\log p_{\max}\). The additive shift leaves \(G\) unchanged. In `continue-weak-oertel.txt`, \(\mathsf I\) is \(I\), and its parity array \(\bar r\) is the explicit array below; that source's different quantity \(\mathcal A=I+G\) is not denoted by \(H\) here. The construction below imposes no optimizing selector.

For \(\mathbf b\in\{0,1\}^n\), let \(\pi_{\mathbf b}=\sum_{\mathbf I\equiv\mathbf b\pmod2}p_{\mathbf I}\) and \(W_{\mathbf b}=W\pi_{\mathbf b}\). The explicit array

\[
r_{\mathbf J,\mathbf I}
=\frac{p_{\mathbf I}p_{2\mathbf J-\mathbf I}}{\pi_{\mathbf I\bmod2}}
\qquad(\mathbf J,\mathbf I\in D)
\]

belongs to \(\mathcal F(p)\). Every denominator displayed here is positive. Its target support is exactly \(D\), and it satisfies

\[
\begin{aligned}
H(r)&=S(p)-S(\pi),\\
G(r)+I(r)+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p)&=S(\pi)\le n\log2,\\
0\le G(r)&\le n\log2-S(q)+H(r).
\end{aligned}
\]

The construction, these identities and inequalities, its full target support, and the component formulas below remain valid under the weaker assumption that every same-parity pair of positive sites has an integral midpoint in \(D\) satisfying \(w_{(\mathbf I+\mathbf K)/2}\ge\sqrt{w_{\mathbf I}w_{\mathbf K}}\).

For every unordered distinct same-parity pair \(E=\{\mathbf I,\mathbf K\}\), give its midpoint target \(\mathbf J=(\mathbf I+\mathbf K)/2\) the component mass \(x_E=w_{\mathbf I}w_{\mathbf K}/W_{\mathbf I\bmod2}\), with barycentric coefficients \(1/2,1/2\). Include the singleton \(E=\{\mathbf I\}\) at target \(\mathbf I\), with mass \(x_E=w_{\mathbf I}^2/W_{\mathbf I\bmod2}\). The original logarithmic component cost of accepted fact `488f0a583886b5fc` is

\[
G_{\{\mathbf I,\mathbf K\}}
=\frac{\phi_{\mathbf I}+\phi_{\mathbf K}}2-\phi_{(\mathbf I+\mathbf K)/2}
=\log\frac{w_{(\mathbf I+\mathbf K)/2}}{\sqrt{w_{\mathbf I}w_{\mathbf K}}},
\qquad G_{\{\mathbf I\}}=0.
\]

The archived pair cost called \(L_{\mathbf I,\mathbf K}\) is this \(G_{\{\mathbf I,\mathbf K\}}\), not the continuous-dimension root cost. Charge each incident source the full component mass. With all targets included simultaneously, the exact capacity, mass, and cost formulas are

\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{E:\mathbf I\in E}x_E&=w_{\mathbf I}\qquad(\mathbf I\in D),\\
M_{\mathrm{all}}:=\sum_Ex_E
&=\frac12\left(W+\sum_{\mathbf I\in D}\frac{w_{\mathbf I}^2}{W_{\mathbf I\bmod2}}\right),
\qquad \frac W2\le M_{\mathrm{all}}\le W,\\
\sum_Ex_EG_E
&=\frac W2G(r)
=\frac W2\bigl(S(\pi)-I(r)-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p)\bigr)
\le\frac W2n\log2.
\end{aligned}
\]

For actual positive-volume fibers \(C_{\mathbf I}\subset\mathbb R^d\) of a convex body, these charges can have uniform source marginals: at each source their sum is exactly \(\mathcal L^d|_{C_{\mathbf I}}\), including when components at different targets use that source.

The coefficient-one inequality is sharp among strictly positive universal coefficients. Precisely, for every \(0<c<1\), choose an integer \(m\ge2\) such that

\[
m\log2>\frac{1+4c}{\min\{c,1-c\}},\qquad \varepsilon=2^{-m}.
\]

On \(D=\{-1,0,1,2\}\subset\mathbb Z\), set \(p_{-1}=p_2=\varepsilon/2\) and \(p_0=p_1=(1-\varepsilon)/2\), with all other values zero. These are the complete integer fiber lengths of a rational planar convex body with total mixed volume one. Every feasible array for this table satisfies

\[
G(r)>c\bigl(\log2-S(q)+H(r)\bigr).
\]

Coefficient zero is a degenerate exception: the diagonal array always has \(G=0\). Thus the sharpness assertion concerns strictly positive coefficients, rather than a minimum over all nonnegative coefficients.

Finally, the normalized rows of the explicit parity array need not be log-concave. For the complete uniform table \(p_i=1/5\) on \(\{0,1,2,3,4\}\), its normalized row at target \(2\), in that source order, is \((1/6,1/4,1/6,1/4,1/6)\). In particular, neither a bound of \(2^n\) on the number of its targets nor global log-concavity of its normalized rows holds in general.
